opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's interesting, because for a long time those thought experiments were exactly that: thought experiments. Searle's Chinese room was meant to be a hypothetical: imagine a system that could produce perfectly fluent Chinese just by following rules, without understanding anything. And now we have systems that, at least on the surface, look a lot like that. They produce remarkably fluent language, and people are asking, "Is there any understanding in there, or is it just symbol manipulation?"

I don't think the analogy is perfect, though. Searle imagined a rulebook that was essentially complete, one that handled every situation flawlessly. What we actually see with large language models is that they're impressive, but they also make very strange errors. They fail in ways that suggest they don't have the kind of robust, flexible concepts that humans have. So in a sense, the systems themselves give us some empirical evidence that Searle's hypothetical didn't. We can probe them. We can test whether their "understanding" generalizes to new situations, whether it's sensitive to things that shouldn't matter, like small changes in wording, and so on.

With philosophical zombies, the idea is a being that behaves exactly like a human but has no inner experience. I tend to be a bit wary of that framing, because it rests on the assumption that you could have perfectly humanlike behavior with nothing going on inside. I'm not sure that's coherent. And again, current systems aren't behaviorally identical to humans. When you look closely, the behavior diverges.

So what I'd say is that these thought experiments were useful for sharpening our intuitions, but now we have the luxury, and the responsibility, of actually doing science on the question. Rather than arguing from armchair intuitions about whether a machine could understand, we can ask: what do we mean by understanding? What capabilities should it confer? Can we design experiments that test for those capabilities in a way that isn't fooled by memorization or surface statistics? To me, that's a much more productive way forward than relitigating the Chinese room.

r001.rationale: It describes the Chinese room as producing perfectly fluent Chinese and handling every situation flawlessly, and a philosophical zombie as behaving exactly like a human.

r002.rationale: It says current systems make strange errors, lack robust and flexible human concepts, and are not behaviorally identical to humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think those thought experiments are more useful than people often give them credit for, but maybe not in the way they were originally intended. Searle's Chinese room was meant to show that syntax alone can't give you semantics, that manipulating symbols according to rules doesn't amount to understanding. And a lot of people in AI dismissed it, and I think partly rightly, because the "systems reply" is pretty compelling. The person in the room doesn't understand Chinese, but maybe the whole system does, and our intuitions about what a room full of paper can or can't do just aren't very reliable.

But what's interesting to me is that large language models have made the Chinese room feel much less hypothetical. We actually have systems now that produce extremely fluent, contextually appropriate language, and we're all having the argument Searle anticipated. Does this thing understand anything, or is it, as some people put it, a very sophisticated version of the room? And I don't think the answer is obvious in either direction. I'm skeptical of people who confidently say these systems understand in the way we do, and I'm also skeptical of people who confidently say they understand nothing. The honest answer is that we don't have a good scientific theory of understanding, so we're arguing from intuitions.

The philosophical zombie case is a little different. That's about consciousness, about whether there could be something behaviorally identical to us with nothing going on inside. I tend to think that's less relevant to current AI, because we're not even close to behavioral equivalence. These systems are brittle in ways that are very un-human. They fail on simple variations of problems they've just solved, they're wildly sensitive to prompt wording, and so on. So I'd actually resist the framing that we have zombies on our hands. What we have is something that is humanlike in some narrow respects and very alien in others.

What I keep coming back to is that we tend to assume capabilities travel together the way they do in people. If a person can write a fluent essay about a topic, we assume they can reason about it, answer odd questions about it, apply it in a new setting. Those assumptions break down with these systems, and I think that's actually the more important lesson. The thought experiments are useful because they force us to ask what we mean by understanding. But the systems themselves are telling us that understanding may not be one thing, and that our concepts, which were built around humans, might just not carve these systems at the right joints.

r001.rationale: The response describes the Chinese room as rule-based symbol manipulation and says a philosophical zombie would be behaviorally identical to us, but it does not identify robust human-like performance as a stipulated feature of both thought experiments.

r002.rationale: The response says current systems are “not even close to behavioral equivalence” and describes their brittle, un-human failures, clearly stating they have not achieved robust human-like performance.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think these thought experiments bring up an important distinction between behaving as if you understand something and actually understanding it. The Chinese room asks whether manipulating symbols according to rules is sufficient for understanding. And with language models, that question feels much more concrete: we have systems that can produce remarkably convincing language, but what does that tell us about what they understand?

I don’t think the thought experiment settles the question. You can argue that the person in the room doesn’t understand Chinese, but perhaps the whole system does. Then you’re back to asking what understanding consists of and how you would recognize it.

Philosophical zombies raise a somewhat different issue, which is subjective experience. I think it’s useful to separate that from understanding. A system might have some understanding of the world without having conscious experience. Fluent conversation alone doesn’t establish either one.

For me, the more productive approach is to ask specific questions: Can these systems apply a concept in a genuinely new situation? Can they handle changes that wouldn’t confuse a person? Where does their apparent understanding break down? That gives us something we can investigate, even if it doesn’t resolve the philosophical questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses convincing language and the Chinese room but does not identify robust human-like performance as a stipulated feature of these thought experiments.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that current AI systems have not achieved robust human-like performance; it only says fluent conversation does not establish understanding or consciousness.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think those thought experiments are useful for getting us to ask what we mean by understanding. In the Chinese room, somebody follows rules for manipulating Chinese symbols without knowing what they mean, and the question is whether producing the right answers is sufficient for understanding. With large language models, that question feels much more concrete than it used to.

But I don’t think the thought experiment settles the issue. Saying that the person inside the room doesn’t understand Chinese doesn’t necessarily tell us what the whole system understands. And describing a language model as “just predicting the next word” doesn’t, by itself, establish what it can or cannot learn through that process. We have to study its behavior, its internal representations, and where its abilities break down.

Philosophical zombies raise a somewhat different question: could something behave exactly like a conscious person without having any subjective experience? I don’t know how we would resolve that empirically. I tend to focus on questions where we can make progress: Can these systems form concepts that generalize? Can they apply what they’ve learned in unfamiliar situations? How robust is their understanding? Those questions don’t solve consciousness, but they help us get beyond either assuming that fluent language proves a humanlike mind or assuming that computation rules one out.

r001.rationale: The response describes symbol manipulation in the Chinese room and a zombie behaving exactly like a conscious person, but it does not identify robust human-like performance as a stipulated feature of both thought experiments.

r002.rationale: The response raises questions about AI abilities and cautions against equating fluent language with a humanlike mind, but it does not state that current AI systems have not yet achieved robust human-like performance.
